title: Karaoke: Tuesday Night Fever
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore karaoke: their personal experiences, the Japanese origins of the term "kara-okey" (empty orchestra) in Osaka in the early 1950s, and Daisuke Inoue's Daisuke "Juke Eight" machine in Kobe. The episode covers the spread to Osaka and Tokyo, Roberto del Rosario's 1975 Philippine patent, Kenji Takagi and Earl Glick bringing karaoke to America with the Singing Machine in 1982, the Frank Sinatra anecdote, Dimples in Burbank as America's first karaoke bar, Sing Along in New York in 1987, the role of karaoke jockeys, American Idol and Lost in Translation reviving interest, the Duets movie, licensing and copyright fees, removed songs, home and solo karaoke (wankara, Smule), and "my Way" related killings. The episode closes with a listener mail about a fifteen-year-old fan and a correction about elephant seals.

segments.title: Opening banter about karaoke experiences
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trade personal karaoke stories, including private K-box rooms, live piano karaoke in Manhattan, stage fright, and song choices.

segments.title: Origin of the term kataoke and Daisuke Inoue
segments.summary: The hosts explain that kara-okey means empty orchestra, a term from a 1950s Osaka strike. They then describe Daisuke Inoue, a Kobe musician who created the Juke Eight, the first karaoke machine, and the early spread of his machines in Kobe.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Sponsor break read during the episode.

segments.title: Karaoke spreads to Osaka and Tokyo; patent decisions
segments.summary: Karaoke takes off in Osaka and Tokyo. Inoue did not patent the Juke Eight, and the hosts discuss the patent system. They mention Roberto del Rosario's 1975 Philippine patent and the history of K. T. Takagi.

segments.title: Karaoke comes to America
segments.summary: Takagi and Earl Glick, who met on a cruise ship, bring karaoke machines to the United States via the Singing Machine. Early public demonstrations were met with boos, and the hosts recount an anecdote about Frank Sinatra.

segments.title: Dimples, Sing Along, and the karaoke jockey
segments.summary: Dimples in Burbank is described as America's first widely known karaoke bar, with stage performance and lyric books. Sing Along in New York is credited with popularizing karaoke in America and introducing the karaoke jockey. CD+G technology is also covered.

segments.title: American Idol, Lost in Translation, and the 1990s
segments.summary: Karaoke declined in the 1990s, then was revived by American Idol and by the Lost in Translation karaoke scene. The hosts also discuss the film Duets.

segments.title: Licensing, copyright, solo karaoke, and my Way incidents
segments.summary: The hosts describe the fees and licensing involved in karaoke, lawsuits, songs removed from catalogs, home and solo karaoke such as wankara and Smule, and reported violence linked to songs such as My Way.

segments.title: Listener mail
segments.summary: A fifteen-year-old listener writes in praising the show, and a listener correction about elephant seals is read.
